catalog_quote: For understanding of the Sogdian phonology and morphology, the so-called “rhythmic law” is of vital importance (Sims-Williams, 1981a, 1984, 1989, pp. 181-82). According to this law, the retention or loss of proto-Sogdian final vowels depends on whether they bore a stress; in its turn, the position of the stress in words of more than one syllable is determined by the quantity of those syllables: all stems in Sogdian, whether nominal or verbal, containing a long vowel are heavy and bear a stress, while a stress falls on the endings of light stems that consist only of short vowel(s). In what follows, light stems are written with a final hyphen (e.g., wn- [wan-] “to do”) to distinguish them from heavy stems (e.g., wyn [wēn] “to see”). ... The rhythmic law shows that a syllable containing a simple vowel followed by a rhotacized or nasal vowel is treated as heavy, e.g., maərγ (mrγ) “forest,” …

audit.reasoning: Quote check: the deciding Yoshida (EIr 2016) quotation is verbatim in the archive-capture text we hold at the stated section, and the Skjaervo corroboration is verbatim in the held scanned (page is 10, not 9, by footer position: cosmetic). Deciding source is a specialist encyclopaedia description restating Sims-Williams 1984; for an extinct language with reconstructed prosody this is effectively the field consensus, and two further open sources downloaded now (Gershevitch 1954 GMS §484-485, §168; Novak 2013 diss. pp. 75-76) state the same light/heavy-stem stress rule with the same heavy class (long vowel, plus V+nasal/V+r clusters, excluding r from old vocalic r).
